drug_class: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor (also classified as a diuretic)
purpose: Acetazolamide is used to treat glaucoma (high pressure in the eye), certain types of seizures, and altitude sickness. It is also sometimes used to reduce fluid buildup in the body. Your doctor may prescribe it for one or more of these reasons.
how_it_works: Your body has an enzyme called carbonic anhydrase that helps control fluid and acid levels. Acetazolamide blocks this enzyme, which reduces the production of fluid in the eye, helps balance acid levels in the blood to control seizures, and helps your kidneys release extra fluid through urine. Think of it as turning down a faucet that produces unwanted fluid or chemicals in the body.
common_side_effects: You may notice increased urination, a tingling or numbness feeling in your hands, feet, or face, loss of appetite, an upset stomach, nausea, drowsiness, or a metallic taste in your mouth. Carbonated drinks like soda may taste flat or strange while you are taking this medicine.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to sulfa drugs, as acetazolamide is related to that family. Do not take it if you have severe kidney or liver disease. Stay well hydrated because this medicine can increase your risk of kidney stones. It can also lower potassium levels in your blood, so your doctor may monitor your lab work. Avoid it if you are pregnant unless your doctor specifically recommends it.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on what condition is being treated. For altitude sickness, a typical dose is 125 to 250 mg taken by mouth twice a day, starting one to two days before going to high altitude. For glaucoma or seizures, doses generally range from 250 mg to 1000 mg per day, divided into smaller doses. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions for your situation.
